title: RSI / Airway
subtitle: Preoxygenation, intubation, and failed-airway setup
inKit: ETT 7.0-7.5 for most adults, 8.0 for large males; test the cuff
Malleable stylet, pre-shaped: hockey stick or gentle curve
10 mL syringe for the cuff
Laryngoscope handle, Mac 3 and Mac 4 blades; check the light before the patient arrives
Water-soluble or lidocaine lubricant for stylet tip and distal ETT
Colorimetric CO2 detector
Bite block or sized oral airway
Tape or commercial tube holder
outsideKit: Video laryngoscope at the bedside before the paralytic
BVM with PEEP valve and O2 reservoir
Nasal cannula at 15 L/min for apneic oxygenation during laryngoscopy
Yankauer suction on, tested, at the right side of the head
Continuous waveform capnography, not colorimetric alone
RSI drugs: induction agent and paralytic drawn, labeled, dose read aloud
Post-intubation sedation ready before the paralytic: propofol, ketamine, or fentanyl plus midazolam infusion
Ventilator set: TV 6-8 mL/kg IBW, rate 14, FiO2 100%, PEEP 5
Cardiac monitor
commonlyForgotten: Nasal cannula left on under the BVM during laryngoscopy
PEEP valve on the BVM before preoxygenation
Waveform capnography - colorimetric gives false positives in low-flow and cardiac arrest states
Suction on before the first bag-mask breath
Post-intubation sedation drawn and labeled - paralytic wears off in 10-15 min
Second ETT, different size
patientSetup: Ramp until the external auditory meatus is level with the sternal notch, especially in obesity and pregnancy: blankets, ramp pillow or scoop
Bed at the intubator's standing working height
IV patent on flush before any medication
Monitoring: waveform SpO2, waveform ETCO2, BP every 2 min, cardiac telemetry
Roles assigned before induction: BVM, drugs, cricoid if used; brief aloud
Say the plan before the paralytic: primary airway, backup device, surgical rescue
sterileSetup: Clean technique, clean gloves
Keep the distal 10 cm of the ETT and the cuff uncontaminated
Mayo stand: ETT and stylet shaped, syringe on, lubricant applied; blade on, light checked
Backup blade (different size or video) on the Mayo stand or within reach
Yankauer uncapped at the right side of the head before induction
backupEquipment: Bougie (Eschmann stylet) - in hand or on mayo stand; use at first difficult view, not after repeated failed attempts
Video laryngoscope - in the room before paralytic given
Supraglottic airway (LMA i-gel or King LT) - 'can't intubate, can oxygenate' bridge device
Surgical airway kit (cric tray) - in the room before RSI begins; indication is CICO
Difficult airway cart location known to everyone in the room before induction begins
references: Walls RM, Murphy MF, et al. Manual of Emergency Airway Management, 5th ed. Lippincott 2018.
Brown CA 3rd, Bair AE, Pallin DJ, Walls RM. Rapid Sequence Intubation for Patients in the Emergency Department. Ann Emerg Med. 2021.
Weingart SD, Levitan RM. Preoxygenation and prevention of desaturation during emergency airway management. Ann Emerg Med. 2012;59(3):165–175.
ACEP Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Management of the Difficult Airway 2013.

title: Surgical Airway (Cric)
subtitle: Can't intubate, can't oxygenate — front-of-neck access
inKit: Scalpel, #20 or #10 blade
Tracheal (cric) hook - holds the inferior thyroid cartilage cephalad while the tube passes
Curved clamp (Kelly) to blunt-dissect and dilate the membrane opening
6.0 cuffed ETT or 6.0 cuffed cric tube
10 mL syringe, pre-charged with air on the field for cuff inflation
Yankauer with suction tubing
Cloth tape or suture to secure the tube
outsideKit: Suction on at the bedside
BVM on O2, ready to ventilate
Waveform capnography
Headlamp or procedure light, not overhead light alone
Second person to stabilize the larynx and hold neutral cervical alignment in trauma
commonlyForgotten: Headlamp
Suction before you cut
Cric hook in before the tube
Confirm with waveform capnography, not colorimetric - low-output states give false negatives
Horizontal incision through the membrane after the vertical skin incision
patientSetup: Shoulder roll to extend the neck; no hyperextension in trauma - inline cervical stabilization
Landmarks before cutting: thyroid notch, down the midline to the soft space - the cricothyroid membrane
Larynx stabilized: non-dominant thumb and middle finger on the thyroid cartilage, index finger on the membrane
Right-handed operator on the patient's right
Semi-elective: mark the membrane with a skin marker; emergency: finger stabilization
Remove neck jewelry; loosen the collar or cervical collar before prep
sterileSetup: Betadine or chlorhexidine over the anterior neck if time permits; in CICO, clean gloves and proceed immediately
Sterile drape if time permits
Mayo stand: scalpel, cric hook, clamp, tube and syringe, suction, gauze
Suction next to the working field
backupEquipment: Needle cricothyrotomy (14g angiocath): temporizing bridge for maximum 30-45 min with jet ventilation — do not delay surgical cric if jet ventilation is unavailable
Melker percutaneous cric kit (Seldinger technique): alternative if scalpel cric not within operator's trained skill set
Video laryngoscope: one final attempt may be reasonable in selected scenarios before declaring CICO
references: Walls RM, Murphy MF, et al. Manual of Emergency Airway Management, 5th ed. Lippincott 2018.
Frerk C, Mitchell VS, McNarry AF, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2015;115(6):827–848.
Duggan LV, et al. Cricothyrotomy for emergency airway. N Engl J Med. 2021;385:e42.

title: Central Venous Catheter
subtitle: Triple-lumen CVC: IJ, subclavian, or femoral under ultrasound
inKit: Triple-lumen CVC: 15-16 cm IJ or subclavian, 20 cm femoral
Introducer needle, 18g
Guidewire, J-tip 0.035"; track the depth mark at the skin throughout
Vessel dilator
1% lidocaine, 5 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles
10 mL syringe for aspiration and flushing
Sterile 4x4 gauze
Large sterile drapes and fenestrated drape
Chlorhexidine applicators ×2 minimum
3-0 silk on a straight needle, or StatLock
Heparin-lock caps ×3, one per lumen
Transparent occlusive dressing, with or without Biopatch
outsideKit: Ultrasound, linear probe 10-15 MHz
Sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Sterile gown
Extra chlorhexidine applicators - one kit stick is not enough
Cardiac monitor during wire passage: ectopy means wire in the RV - pull back
10 mL saline flushes ×3, one per lumen
Chest X-ray before first use: tip in the SVC, no pneumothorax
Blood culture bottles if drawing cultures at placement
commonlyForgotten: Sterile probe cover and sterile gel - non-sterile gel does not substitute
Mark the wire depth at the skin before dilating
Wire in the vein on ultrasound before the dilator passes
All three lumens primed with saline before suturing and dressing
Chest X-ray before the first medication
patientSetup: IJ: Trendelenburg 15-20 degrees, head turned away, roll under the ipsilateral shoulder
Subclavian: roll under the scapulae (not mid-back), arm tucked at the side, slight Trendelenburg
Femoral: leg extended and externally rotated, table flat
Time-out before draping: patient ID, site, side, allergies (especially chlorhexidine), procedure
Maximal barrier precautions: cap, mask with eye protection, sterile gown, sterile gloves
Non-sterile assistant for ultrasound, medications, specimen tubes, sharps
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine back-and-forth scrub for 30 seconds; full 2 minutes to dry
Betadine if chlorhexidine allergy; 2 minutes to dry
Sterile drape head to toe, fenestrated over the site
Mayo stand in order: lidocaine syringe, introducer needle, guidewire, dilator, catheter, caps
Sterile probe cover on before skin puncture; no scanning without it
backupEquipment: Introducer sheath (Cordis): if 8.5 Fr large-bore access needed for resuscitation, emergent RHC, or transvenous pacer passage
Dialysis catheter (Vas-Cath): if CRRT or acute hemodialysis is anticipated
Two large-bore peripheral IVs as bridge if central access is delayed
Arterial line if continuous hemodynamic monitoring is simultaneously required
references: McGee DC, Gould MK. Preventing Complications of Central Venous Catheterization. N Engl J Med. 2003;348:1123–1133.
Marschall J, et al. SHEA/IDSA Practice Recommendation: Strategies to Prevent CLABSI. Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol. 2014;35(7):753–771.
Hind D, et al. Ultrasonic locating devices for central venous cannulation: meta-analysis. BMJ. 2003;327:361.
O'Grady NP, et al. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections. CDC/HICPAC 2011.

title: Chest Tube / Thoracostomy
subtitle: Large-bore drainage for hemothorax, pneumothorax, or empyema
inKit: Chest tube: 28-32 Fr for hemothorax, 20-24 Fr for uncomplicated pneumothorax - choose before opening
Large curved Kelly clamps ×2: one to dissect, one to pass the tube
Scalpel, #10 blade, or #21 for a large incision
20 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles for lidocaine
0 silk or 0 Prolene on a large curved needle for anchoring
Chlorhexidine applicators
Large sterile drape
Petroleum gauze (Xeroform) for the exit site
Silk or cloth tape for anchoring
outsideKit: Pleural drainage system (e.g. Pleur-evac), water seal filled with sterile water before connecting
Sterile connector tubing, chest tube to drainage system
Wall suction to the drainage system at -20 cmH2O
Lidocaine 1-2%, at least 20-30 mL for adult infiltration - most kits hold only 10 mL
IV morphine or fentanyl
Chest X-ray right after placement for tube position
Pulse oximetry and cardiac monitor through the procedure and recovery
Non-sterile assistant for tubing, drainage system, suction
commonlyForgotten: Drainage system filled to the water-seal line before connecting
Petroleum gauze at the exit site
Adequate analgesia before the incision
After connecting: suction active, water seal oscillating
Horizontal mattress anchor suture - tape alone is not enough
patientSetup: Ipsilateral arm above the head (hand behind the head or draped overhead)
Safe triangle: lateral pectoralis border anteriorly, mid-axillary line posteriorly, 4th-5th ICS superiorly
Mark the site before prep when possible
Alert patient: head of bed 30-45°
IV opioid 5-10 min before prep; local at the site with a rib periosteum block
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine axilla to midline, 3 complete passes; 2 min to dry
Sterile drape, neck to waist
Sterile gown and gloves, mask, eye protection
Mayo stand in order: lidocaine syringe, scalpel, clamps ×2, chest tube (distal end clamped), suture, petroleum gauze
backupEquipment: Pigtail catheter (14-16 Fr Seldinger kit): for uncomplicated pneumothorax or free-flowing effusion when large-bore tube is not indicated
Needle decompression (14g angiocath, 2nd ICS MCL): for tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise — do not wait for chest tube in arrest
CT surgery or thoracic consult: initial hemothorax >1500 mL OR ongoing >200 mL/hr
references: Dev SP, Nascimento B Jr, Simone C, Chien V. Chest-Tube Insertion. N Engl J Med. 2007;357:e15.
Mowery NT, et al. EAST Practice Management Guidelines for Management of Hemothorax and Occult Pneumothorax. J Trauma. 2011;70(2):510–518.
Laws D, Neville E, Duffy J; BTS Pleural Disease Group. BTS guidelines for the insertion of a chest drain. Thorax. 2003;58 Suppl 2:ii53–59.

title: Arterial Line

Guidewire, 0.018" or 0.025"
10 mL syringe to confirm aspiration
Transparent occlusive dressing
StatLock or 3-0 suture
Chlorhexidine applicator
Sterile mini-drape or sterile towel
outsideKit: Pressure transducer tubing kit - ordered separately
Pressure bag: 500 mL NS at 300 mmHg, tubing primed with no air bubbles
Transducer holder, pole or arm mount
Wrist roll: rolled gauze or folded towel
Cloth tape to hold the wrist dorsiflexed
Monitor with the arterial channel selected and scaled
Transducer zeroed at the phlebostatic axis (4th ICS, mid-axillary line) before the line goes in
commonlyForgotten: Wrist dorsiflexed before prep - the radial artery is 30-50% more superficial and palpable in extension
Tubing primed and transducer zeroed before the catheter goes in
Suture or StatLock - tape alone is not enough
Arterial waveform with a dicrotic notch before the dressing
Elective cases: Allen's test for ulnar collateral flow before radial occlusion if the patient cannot tolerate hand ischemia
patientSetup: Awake, cooperative patient: non-dominant wrist preferred
Wrist dorsiflexed 45-60° over the roll; tape the index, middle and ring fingers back without occluding circulation
Radial pulse 1-2 cm proximal to the flexor wrist crease; mark with a thumbnail
Arm at or below heart level
Ultrasound: linear probe 10-15 MHz, transverse over the radial artery
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine over the wrist; let it dry
Sterile mini-drape or towel over the wrist
Sterile gloves
Mayo stand: catheter assembled, syringe attached, dressing open
Primed, zeroed pressure tubing handed onto the field before the catheter goes in
backupEquipment: Ultrasound-guided placement (linear probe with sterile cover): use when radial pulse is weak, absent, or after two failed palpation attempts

Brzezinski M, Luisetti T, London MJ. Radial artery cannulation: a comprehensive review of recent anatomic and physiologic investigations. Anesth Analg. 2009;109(6):1763–1781.
Slogoff S, et al. Complications of radial artery catheterization. Anesth Analg. 1983;62(2):180–184.

title: Lumbar Puncture
subtitle: CSF sampling for meningitis, SAH workup, and ICP measurement
inKit: Spinal needle: 22-25g Sprotte/Whitacre pencil-point with its introducer - the default for adults; less post-LP headache, harder first pass
Stylet in while the needle advances; out only once the tip is intrathecal
CSF tubes ×4, labeled 1-4
Three-way stopcock for opening pressure
Manometer - some kits omit it
Sterile drapes and fenestrated drape
Chlorhexidine applicators ×3 minimum
1% lidocaine, 10 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles for skin and deep infiltration
Sterile 4x4s and bandage
outsideKit: Ultrasound, linear probe 10-15 MHz, to find the interspace in obese, elderly or scoliotic patients
Fluoroscopy (IR) if bedside attempts fail
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen, not an opioid, 30-60 min before to reduce post-LP headache
Labs ordered before starting: cell count (tubes 1 and 4), glucose, protein, Gram stain and culture; xanthochromia if SAH suspected
Extra tubes for cytology, TB, fungal antigen or unusual studies - 3-8 mL more
Non-sterile assistant to hold the patient flexed and pass tubes without touching the field
commonlyForgotten: All 4 tubes labeled before opening the kit
Opening pressure before removing any CSF; closing pressure too
Stylet back in before withdrawing the needle
Cell count on tube 4 as well as tube 1: RBCs falling from tube 1 to 4 favor a traumatic tap over true pleocytosis
Chlorhexidine fully dry before the spinal needle - wet chlorhexidine is neurotoxic
patientSetup: Lateral decubitus: knees to chest, chin tucked, back arched toward the operator; pillow between the knees keeps the spine horizontal
Or seated, leaning forward over a pillow on the bedside table, arms crossed and supported - better spinal flexion in obese patients
L3-L4 or L4-L5; the iliac crests are at about the L4 spinous process
Mark the interspace with a thumbnail indent before prep
Lateral approach: operator seated, bed at working height
Assistant holds the patient flexed - movement during needle passage is the most common cause of a bloody tap
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine in widening circles ×3; full 2 minutes to dry before the spinal needle
Sterile drapes, fenestrated over the interspace
Sterile gloves and mask
In order: lidocaine syringe, exploring needle, spinal needle, stopcock and manometer, tubes
Spinal needle bevel parallel to the dural fibers (facing the flank in lateral position) to reduce headache
backupEquipment: Ultrasound-guided approach: use when bony landmarks are not palpable; mark interspace with probe before prepping
Fluoroscopy-guided LP (IR): for severe obesity, scoliosis, prior lumbar surgery, or multiple failed bedside attempts
20g Quincke cutting needle: the fallback when no atraumatic needle is stocked; higher post-LP headache incidence
Blood patch (anesthesia consult): for refractory post-LP headache that does not resolve with caffeine and supine positioning
references: Straus SE, Thorpe KE, Holroyd-Leduc J. How do I perform a lumbar puncture and analyze the results to diagnose bacterial meningitis? JAMA. 2006;296(16):2012–2022.
van Crevel H, Hijdra A, de Gans J. Lumbar puncture and the risk of herniation: when should we first perform CT? J Neurol. 2002;249(2):129–137.
Armon C, Evans RW; Therapeutics and Technology Assessment Subcommittee. Addendum to assessment: prevention of post-lumbar puncture headaches. Neurology. 2005;65(4):510–512.

title: Thoracentesis

Drainage bag (1000-1500 mL) or vacuum bottles ×2

Chlorhexidine applicators ×3
1% lidocaine, 10 mL syringe, 25g and 22g needles - infiltrate generously to the parietal pleura
10 mL and 20 mL syringes for aspiration
Sterile specimen cups ×3
Sterile 4x4s and adhesive bandage
outsideKit: Ultrasound, curvilinear 3.5-5 MHz
Sterile probe cover for real-time needle guidance
Lab tubes, ordered before starting: LDH, protein, glucose, cell count, Gram stain and culture, cytology
Heparinized syringe for pleural fluid pH if parapneumonic effusion suspected
Chest X-ray or ultrasound after the procedure for pneumothorax
Pulse oximetry and cardiac monitor during and for 1 hour after
Non-sterile assistant to hold the patient seated and pass specimen containers
commonlyForgotten: Mark with ultrasound immediately before the procedure - not hours earlier, not before a position change
No more than 1000-1500 mL at one sitting - re-expansion pulmonary edema
Needle over the top of the rib - the neurovascular bundle runs along the inferior margin
pH in suspected parapneumonic effusion: below 7.20 needs tube drainage, not just sampling
Bevel down, away from the lung, during aspiration to reduce pneumothorax risk
patientSetup: Seated, leaning forward onto a pillow on the overbed table
Arms crossed and supported to keep the scapulae retracted
Posterior approach, 2 interspaces below the top of the effusion on ultrasound, above the 9th rib to avoid the diaphragm
Skin-mark right after scanning; thumbnail indent as a second reference
Cannot sit up: lateral decubitus, effusion side dependent
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine ×3 passes over the posterior chest; 2 minutes to dry
Large sterile drape, fenestrated over the site
Sterile gloves and mask

Drainage bag below the patient before aspiration begins
backupEquipment: Pigtail catheter (14-16 Fr Seldinger kit): for prolonged drainage over days, loculated effusion, or empyema not draining through needle
Chest tube (24-28 Fr): if empyema is confirmed or frank pus encountered

Light RW. Parapneumonic effusions and empyema. Proc Am Thorac Soc. 2006;3(1):75–80.
ACCP Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Lung Cancer, 3rd ed. Pleural Effusion section. 2013.

title: Pericardiocentesis
subtitle: Emergency relief of pericardial tamponade by subxiphoid or apical approach
inKit: Pericardiocentesis needle: 18g spinal, 6-9 cm, or commercial kit
Seldinger kit: 0.035" J-tip guidewire, pigtail or straight drainage catheter
50-60 mL syringes ×2
Three-way stopcock
Sterile drapes and chlorhexidine applicators
1-2% lidocaine, 10 mL syringe, 25g needle
ECG alligator clip (V-lead wire) for the needle hub when echo is unavailable
outsideKit: Bedside echo, phased-array or curvilinear 2-5 MHz: effusion size and approach window
Sterile probe cover for real-time echo guidance
12-lead ECG machine for V-lead monitoring if echo is unavailable
Continuous cardiac monitor with rhythm strip throughout
Crash cart at the bedside: defibrillator charged, epinephrine 1 mg and atropine 0.5 mg drawn
Cardiothoracic surgery aware before starting - a surgical pericardial window may be needed if drainage fails
Continuous BP, pulse oximetry, waveform; two running IVs
commonlyForgotten: Echo before the needle: effusion location, size and approach; avoids RV free-wall puncture
Watch V-lead for ST elevation or current of injury - the tip has entered the ventricle; pull back immediately
Do not remove more than 50-100 mL rapidly from a chronic large effusion
Seldinger kit: leave the drain 24-48 hours - tamponade recurrence within hours is common in malignant and purulent effusions
Blood that does not clot: pericardial hemorrhage; blood that clots: needle in a cardiac chamber
patientSetup: Head of bed 30-45 degrees
Choose the window on echo before prep: subxiphoid or apical, by the largest pocket with the least lung in the way
Subxiphoid: just below the xiphoid, needle at 45 degrees toward the left shoulder
Apical: 5th-6th ICS just lateral to the left cardiac border, angled 30 degrees posteriorly and superiorly
Hemodynamically compromised: IV fluid bolus before drainage
Operator on the patient's right for subxiphoid, left for apical
sterileSetup: Chlorhexidine over the subxiphoid or apical site; 2 min to dry
Sterile drapes
Sterile gloves, gown and mask
60 mL syringe on the stopcock at the needle hub before insertion
Alligator clip on the metal needle hub if using ECG guidance
backupEquipment: Cardiothoracic surgery for subxiphoid surgical pericardial window: failed bedside drainage, loculated effusion, trauma with hemopericardium
Pericardiocentesis under fluoroscopy (cardiac cath lab): for difficult anatomy or large loculated effusion
Balloon pericardiotomy (IR): for recurrent malignant effusions requiring definitive window without open surgery

Tsang TS, El-Najdawi EK, Seward JB, et al. Percutaneous echocardiographically guided pericardiocentesis in pediatric patients. Mayo Clin Proc. 1998;73(7):647–652.
Fitch MT, Nicks BA, Pariyadath M, McGinnis HD, Manthey DE. Emergency pericardiocentesis. N Engl J Med. 2012;366:e17.
